claim: The LGMD is a collision-detecting neuron in the grasshopper optic lobe located three synapses away from photoreceptors.
source: the lobula giant movement detector (LGMD, Figure 1A) has been extensively studied: it is an identified neuron of the grasshopper optic lobe located three synapses away from photoreceptors (O'Shea and Williams, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Shea and Williams, 1974.

claim: The LGMD responds maximally to looming stimuli.
source: The LGMD responds maximally to looming stimuli (Schlotterer, 1977; Rind and Simmons, 1992; Hatsopoulos et al., 1995) with a characteristic firing rate profile (Hatsopoulos et al., 1995; Gabbiani et al., 1999) (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1B showing the firing rate profile.

claim: The LGMD's characteristic firing profile has been tightly linked to initiating escape behaviors.
source: This characteristic firing profile is maintained even when an approaching stimulus is embedded in a random motion background, suggesting that the LGMD may be able to effectively segment visual objects (Silva et al., 2015; Yakubowski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fotowat et al., 2011 and Silva et al., 2015; Yakubowski et al., 2016.

claim: The LGMD responds only weakly to a stimulus whose angular size increases linearly in time.
source: In contrast, the LGMD responds only weakly to a stimulus whose angular size increases linearly in time, corresponding to an object decelerating during approach (Hatsopoulos et al., 1995; Simmons and Rind, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hatsopoulos et al., 1995 and Simmons and Rind, 1992.

claim: Dendritic field A receives excitatory inputs originating from each ommatidium on the ipsilateral compound eye in a precise retinotopic projection.
source: The third one, dendritic field A, receives excitatory inputs originating from each ommatidium (facet) on the ipsilateral compound eye in a precise retinotopic projection (Krapp and Gabbiani, 2005; Peron et al., 2009; Zhu and Gabbiani, 2016) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A showing the retinotopic mapping.

claim: Locusts showed a strong behavioral selectivity to spatial coherence, with stimuli less than 50% coherent eliciting no escape jumps.
source: Locusts showed a strong behavioral selectivity to spatial coherence; stimuli with less than 50% spatial coherence elicited no escape jumps, but jump probability increased rapidly with coherence above 50% (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The LGMD's spike count and peak firing rate were lower for 0% coherent than 100% coherent looming stimuli.
source: The LGMD's spike count (p=2.5·10−4, Wilcoxon rank sum, WRS) and peak firing rate (p=1.9·10−4, WRS) were lower for 0% coherent than 100% coherent looming stimuli (N = 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Hyperpolarization of field A produced a characteristic rectifying sag, which was abolished by the HCN channel blocker ZD7288.
source: Hyperpolarization of field A produced a characteristic rectifying sag, which was abolished by the HCN channel blockers ZD7288 (Figure 2B) and Cs+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Sags recorded from field A without HCN channel block were significantly larger and faster than those recorded from other neuronal regions.
source: On average, sags recorded from field A without HCN channel block were significantly larger and faster than those recorded from other neuronal regions (Figure 2D,E; compare Field A control, vs. trunk and Field B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Block of HCN channels by ZD7288 in field A removed the rectifying sags.
source: Similarly, block of HCN channels by ZD7288 in field A removed these sags (Figure 2D,E; compare Field A control vs. ZD7288).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Recordings at different locations within the dendritic trunk and field A revealed an increase in sag with electrotonic distance from the SIZ.
source: Recordings at different locations within the dendritic trunk and field A revealed an increase in sag with electrotonic distance from the SIZ (Figure 2F) suggesting a higher channel density distally in field A.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The HCN channels in field A have an activation curve and time constant similar to that of HCN2 channels.
source: To characterize the channel kinetics, field A dendrites were voltage clamped. As HCN channels are distinctive in their activation range and time course we were able to measure and fit their currents (see Materials and methods; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), revealing an activation curve (Figure 2G) and time constant (Figure 2H) similar to that of HCN2 channels (Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G,H and comparison to literature (Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).

claim: Application of cAMP shifted the half-activation potential of gH from −77.6 ± 3.8 to −73.4 ± 2.2 mV.
source: Application of cAMP shifted the half-activation potential (v1/2) of gH from −77.6 ± 3.8 to −73.4 ± 2.2 mV (mean ±sd; Figure 2G)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: For standard looming stimuli, gH was excitatory with responses reduced by 61% after HCN blockade.
source: For standard looming stimuli, gH was excitatory with responses reduced by 61% after HCN blockade (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Responses to localized luminance transients were similar before and after blockade of gH.
source: Responses to localized luminance transients, however, were similar before and after blockade of gH (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Under control conditions, there was a large increase in LGMD response with stimulus coherence which was reduced after ZD7288 blockade by 42% for coarse looming stimuli.
source: Under control conditions, there was a large increase in LGMD response with stimulus coherence which was reduced after ZD7288 blockade (42% for coarse looming stimuli; Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: For every animal tested, the coherence preference was reduced after gH blockade, decreasing from a median of 0.24 to 0.06 spikes per percent coherence.
source: For every animal tested, the coherence preference was reduced after gH blockade, decreasing from a median of 0.24 to 0.06 spikes per percent coherence (Figure 2L; similar results were observed for the peak firing rate, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: After gH blockade, the mean response to all stimuli fell within ±1 sd of the mean control response to 0% coherence.
source: After blockade, the mean response to all stimuli fell within ±1 sd of the mean control response to 0% coherence (p=0.10; KW).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Jump probabilities at each coherence level strongly correlate with the gH-dependent increase in firing for that coherence level.
source: Next, we compared the jump probabilities at each coherence level (Figure 1F) with the gH-dependent increase in firing for that coherence level (difference between control and HCN block in Figure 2M). This revealed a strong correlation between physiology and behavior (Figure 2N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: Responses to faster looming stimuli showed a smaller gH-dependent increase in firing.
source: Furthermore, responses to faster looming stimuli, which fail to produce escape behaviors before the projected time of collision (Fotowat and Gabbiani, 2007), showed a smaller gH-dependent increase in firing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G and citation to Fotowat and Gabbiani, 2007.

claim: Blocking gH in the LGMD reduced escape behavior by 53% for standard looming stimuli compared to saline injection.
source: Blocking gH in the LGMD reduced escape behavior by 53% for standard looming stimuli compared to saline injection (Figure 3A, left two dots).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The coherence preference was removed by blockade of gH: standard looming stimuli no longer produced a higher percentage of escape than reduced coherence stimuli.
source: The coherence preference was also removed by blockade of gH: standard looming stimuli no longer produced a higher percentage of escape than reduced coherence stimuli (Figure 3A, red dots).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: gH blockade by ZD7288 decreased responses to both standard looming stimuli and 86% coherent stimuli.
source: gH blockade by ZD7288 decreased responses to both standard looming stimuli and 86% coherent stimuli (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The reduction in firing in the freely moving animals was less than that in the restrained preparation (36% and 60%, respectively).
source: The reduction in firing in the freely moving animals was less than that in the restrained preparation (36% and 60%, respectively), which might be due to an incomplete block of gH after stereotactic injection compared to visually guided puffing (see Materials and methods) or differences in arousal state.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from different preparations.

claim: gH increased the resting membrane potential (RMP) by ~6 mV in field A.
source: gH increased the resting membrane potential (RMP) by ~6 mV in field A, which would bring the neuron closer to spike threshold (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Blockade of gH decreased input resistance by 50% and the membrane time constant by 30%.
source: Blockade also revealed gH to decrease input resistance by 50% and the membrane time constant (τm) by 30% (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: After gH blockade, summation from the first to fifth sEPSP increased for all tested delays.
source: After gH blockade, summation from the first to fifth sEPSP increased for all tested delays (Figure 4E; the dashed lines are from the biophysical model described below).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The integrated sEPSPs normalized by the integrated current increased by 77% after gH blockade.
source: Additionally, the integrated sEPSPs normalized by the integrated current increased by 77% (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Neither before nor after gH blockade was supralinear summation ever seen in LGMD dendrites.
source: Neither before nor after gH blockade was supralinear summation ever seen in LGMD dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Application of 4AP increased the resting membrane potential in field A by 2–5 mV.
source: Application of 4AP, either intracellularly or extracellularly, increased the resting membrane potential in field A by 2–5 mV and the spiking response and instantaneous firing rate to standard looming stimuli (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Application of 4AP increased responses to coarse looming stimuli of varying degree of coherence, but responses to fully coherent looming stimuli increased the least.
source: Application of 4AP also increased responses to coarse looming stimuli of varying degree of coherence, but responses to fully coherent looming stimuli increased the least (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: While HCN channels predominantly boosted responses to coherent stimuli, inactivating K+ channels mainly decreased responses to incoherent ones.
source: Thus, while HCN channels predominantly boosted responses to coherent stimuli, inactivating K+ channels mainly decreased responses to incoherent ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from HCN and K+ channel blockade experiments.

claim: Lowering the RMP without the changes to input resistance and membrane time constant caused by gH blockade only produced a modest reduction in coherence preference, with responses to standard looming stimuli reduced by 20% vs. 61% after ZD7288 blockade.
source: However, lowering the RMP without the changes to input resistance and membrane time constant caused by gH blockade (Figure 4B,C) only produced a modest reduction in coherence preference, with responses to standard looming stimuli reduced by 20% vs. 61% after ZD7288 blockade (p=0.03, WRS; see above and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The membrane depolarization systematically decreased with increasing stimulus distance in the control condition, but this effect was abolished after 4AP.
source: This revealed that the membrane depolarization systematically decreased with increasing stimulus distance in the control condition, but this effect was abolished after 4AP (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Throughout stimulus expansion, the more dispersed excitatory inputs were, the less dendritic depolarization they produced in control conditions, a feature absent after 4AP application.
source: Throughout stimulus expansion, the more dispersed excitatory inputs were, the less dendritic depolarization they produced in control conditions, a feature absent after 4AP application (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: For each time window, 4AP increased the depolarization produced in field A by more distant stimuli with an average slope difference of 1.05 mV per degree of visual separation.
source: For each time window, 4AP increased the depolarization produced in field A by more distant stimuli with an average slope difference of 1.05 mV per degree of visual separation (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A model of the LGMD with passive dendrites generated a smaller response to retinotopically arranged looming inputs than the same inputs impinging on random dendritic locations.
source: First, we confirmed that a model of the LGMD with passive dendrites generated a smaller response to retinotopically arranged looming inputs than the same inputs impinging on random dendritic locations both in terms of the mean membrane potential and the instantaneous firing rate (Figure 7A, top and bottom panels, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Adding HCN channels to the dendrites of the model while adjusting the leak conductance to maintain RMP and Ri, also resulted in stronger responses to spatially scrambled inputs.
source: Adding HCN channels to the dendrites of this model while adjusting the leak conductance to maintain RMP and Ri, also resulted in stronger responses to spatially scrambled inputs (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The subsequent addition of inactivating K+ channels in dendritic field A reduced responses to the spatially scrambled inputs, bringing the model in broad agreement with experimental findings.
source: As suggested by the results of Figures 5 and 6, the subsequent addition of inactivating K+ channels in dendritic field A reduced responses to the spatially scrambled inputs, bringing the model in broad agreement with experimental findings (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7C.

claim: During coherent looming stimuli, inputs continue to impinge on nearby dendritic segments for a prolonged period, spreading slowly.
source: During coherent looming stimuli, inputs continue to impinge on nearby dendritic segments for a prolonged period, spreading slowly (Figure 7D, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7D.

claim: With spatially incoherent stimuli, inputs spread out over a much larger region of the dendritic arbor.
source: With spatially incoherent stimuli, inputs spread out over a much larger region of the dendritic arbor (Figure 7D, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The prolonged depolarization generated by a coherent loom causes HCN channels to close and the KD-like channels to inactivate.
source: The prolonged depolarization generated by a coherent loom causes HCN channels to close (Figure 7F, dashed black line) and the KD-like channels to inactivate (Figure 7F, solid black line).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7F.

claim: During spatially incoherent stimuli, HCN channels close less and the KD-like channels across the arbor undergo less inactivation.
source: During spatially incoherent stimuli, however, HCN channels close less and the KD-like channels across the arbor undergo less inactivation (Figure 7F, gray lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7F.

claim: After HCN blockade, the lower resting membrane potential reduces the baseline KD-like channel inactivation.
source: After HCN blockade, the lower resting membrane potential reduces the baseline KD-like channel inactivation (Figure 7F, red line) so that even with spatially coherent inputs the channels never reach the same level of inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7F.

claim: During the last 2 s before collision, the average inactivation of both CaT and KD-like channels increased with stimulus coherence.
source: During the last 2 s before collision, when most firing occurred, the average inactivation of both CaT and KD-like channels increased with stimulus coherence (Figure 7I).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The slope of the best fit line for KD-like inactivation vs. stimulus coherence was three times as steep as that of CaT inactivation.
source: Yet, the slope of the best fit line for KD-like inactivation vs. stimulus coherence was three times as steep as that of CaT inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results.

claim: Despite containing the same conductances and the same passive properties as the full model, the simplified morphology markedly reduced the coherence selectivity.
source: Despite containing the same conductances and the same passive properties as the full model, the simplified morphology markedly reduced the coherence selectivity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Both faster and slower kinetics of HCN closing and KD-like inactivation reduced the coherence selectivity.
source: Simulations were conducted with altered kinetics of HCN closing and KD-like inactivation, and both faster and slower kinetics reduced the coherence selectivity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The model reproduced key experimental results, including the LGMD's preference for spatially coherent inputs and the reduction of this preference after block of gH.
source: More precisely, the model reproduced key experimental results, including the LGMD's preference for spatially coherent inputs and the reduction of this preference after block of gH (Figure 2M; Figure 5D)
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2M and Figure 5D.

claim: The model reproduced the electrotonic and summation effects of gH.
source: the electrotonic and summation effects of gH (Figure 4E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The model reproduced the coherence-dependent increase in firing caused by blocking the inactivating K+ channels and their role in suppressing responses to incoherent stimuli.
source: the coherence-dependent increase in firing caused by blocking the inactivating K+ channels and their role in suppressing responses to incoherent stimuli (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The model did not reproduce quantitatively all experimental results, underestimating the amount of transient firing at high coherence and overestimating its sustained firing.
source: Yet, the model did not reproduce quantitatively all our experimental results: for example, it underestimated the amount of transient firing at high coherence and, vice-versa, overestimated its sustained firing (Figure 7E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1F,G, dashed lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of computational modeling results with experimental data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Excitatory synaptic inputs are segregated by ommatidia and arranged in columnar fashion over an entire visual hemifield.
source: These excitatory synaptic inputs are segregated by ommatidia and arranged in columnar fashion over an entire visual hemifield, so the LGMD's dendritic arbor has access to the entire spatial visual pattern activated by an approaching stimulus.
evidence: The claim is based on the anatomical organization of the LGMD's dendritic field A.

claim: The precise retinotopy of field A means that the spatial pattern of synaptic inputs is directly determined by that of the visual stimulus.
source: The precise retinotopy of field A (Peron et al., 2009; Zhu and Gabbiani, 2016) means that the spatial pattern of synaptic inputs is directly determined by that of the visual stimulus, offering the possibility to experimentally control the synaptic patterning in vivo by changing the spatial aspect of visual stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on the retinotopic organization of field A and is supported by citations to Peron et al., 2009 and Zhu and Gabbiani, 2016.

claim: HCN channels play a central role in the computation of spatial coherence in the LGMD.
source: One channel type linked to dendritic computations in many neural systems, the hyperpolarization-activated cation channel, HCN, plays a central role in this computation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing the effects of HCN channel blockade on coherence selectivity.

claim: Pharmacological block of HCN channels abolishes the neuron's spatial selectivity and impairs the generation of visually guided escape behaviors.
source: Pharmacological block of HCN channels abolishes the neuron's spatial selectivity and impairs the generation of visually guided escape behaviors, making it directly relevant to survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effects of HCN channel blockade on both neural responses and escape behavior.

claim: The interaction of HCN and inactivating K+ channels within active dendrites produces neuronal and behavioral object specificity by discriminating between complex spatiotemporal synaptic activation patterns.
source: Additionally, our results suggest that the interaction of HCN and inactivating K+ channels within active dendrites produces neuronal and behavioral object specificity by discriminating between complex spatiotemporal synaptic activation patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the complementary effects of HCN and K+ channels on coherence selectivity.

claim: Objects approaching on a collision course produce a characteristic visual stimulus on the observer's retina, expanding coherently in all directions with increasing angular velocity.
source: Objects approaching on a collision course or their simulation on a screen, called looming stimuli, produce a characteristic visual stimulus on the observer's retina, expanding coherently in all directions with increasing angular velocity.
evidence: The claim is based on the physics of approaching objects and their visual representation.

claim: Discriminating the retinal pattern of a looming stimulus from that of optic flow or from that of an object approaching on a miss trajectory requires integrating information across many points in time and space.
source: Discriminating this retinal pattern from that of optic flow or from that of an object approaching on a miss trajectory requires integrating information across many points in time and space.
evidence: The claim is based on the computational requirements for discriminating different types of visual motion.

claim: The LGMD is located three synapses away from photoreceptors.
source: it is an identified neuron of the grasshopper optic lobe located three synapses away from photoreceptors (O'Shea and Williams, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Shea and Williams, 1974.

claim: The LGMD's characteristic firing profile is maintained even when an approaching stimulus is embedded in a random motion background.
source: This characteristic firing profile is maintained even when an approaching stimulus is embedded in a random motion background, suggesting that the LGMD may be able to effectively segment visual objects (Silva et al., 2015; Yakubowski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Silva et al., 2015 and Yakubowski et al., 2016.

claim: Synaptic inputs onto the LGMD are physically segregated into three dendritic fields, two of which receive non-retinotopically organized inhibitory inputs.
source: Synaptic inputs onto the LGMD are physically segregated into three dendritic fields, two of which receive non-retinotopically organized inhibitory inputs (Strausfeld and Naessel, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Strausfeld and Naessel, 1981.

claim: None of the known properties of the LGMD or its presynaptic circuitry could explain the spatial selectivity to coherence.
source: None of the known properties of the LGMD or its presynaptic circuitry could explain this spatial selectivity.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of existing knowledge about the LGMD.

claim: Previous experiments showed that the strength of excitatory inputs encodes the temporal characteristics of the approaching object by tracking local changes in luminance independent of their spatial pattern.
source: Previous experiments showed that the strength of excitatory inputs encodes the temporal characteristics of the approaching object by tracking local changes in luminance independent of their spatial pattern (Jones and Gabbiani, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jones and Gabbiani, 2010.

claim: The spatial clustering of synaptic inputs that occurs with coherent stimuli reduced summation in simulations of passive LGMD dendrites.
source: Additionally, the spatial clustering of synaptic inputs that occurs with coherent stimuli reduced summation in simulations of passive LGMD dendrites (Peron et al., 2009), as further elaborated below.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peron et al., 2009.

claim: No active conductances have yet been characterized within the dendrites of field A.
source: The LGMD's selectivity for the spatial characteristics of an approaching object are therefore likely determined by active processing within the dendrites of field A. No active conductances, however, have yet been characterized within these dendrites.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: Evidence suggests that neither the fast Na+ nor Ca2+ channels that produce supralinear summation in other neurons are present in field A dendrites.
source: Evidence suggests that neither the fast Na+ nor Ca2+ channels that produce supralinear summation in other neurons are present there (Jones and Gabbiani, 2010; Peron and Gabbiani, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jones and Gabbiani, 2010 and Peron and Gabbiani, 2009.

claim: Previous experiments suggested putative HCN channels within the LGMD.
source: Since in many cells HCN channels influence dendritic computations, and previous experiments suggested putative HCN channels within the LGMD (Gabbiani and Krapp, 2006), we hypothesized that HCN channels within field A might be involved in discriminating the spatial coherence of approaching objects.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gabbiani and Krapp, 2006.

claim: HCN channels narrow the membrane's temporal and spatial integration window to excitatory synaptic currents over an extended dendritic harbor.
source: Specifically, HCN channels narrow the membrane's temporal and spatial integration window to excitatory synaptic currents over an extended dendritic harbor.
evidence: The claim is based on known properties of HCN channels.

claim: As approaching objects expand toward collision time, the closing of HCN channels could broaden the integration window and thus provide a slow positive feedback mechanism to tune a neuron to the visual stimuli associated with approaching objects.
source: As approaching objects expand toward collision time, the closing of HCN channels could broaden the integration window and thus provide a slow positive feedback mechanism to tune a neuron to the visual stimuli associated with approaching objects.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the properties of HCN channels and the dynamics of looming stimuli.

claim: The LGMD and escape behavior to looming stimuli are tuned to stimulus coherence.
source: Tuning of the LGMD and escape behavior to stimulus coherence
evidence: The claim is implied by the section heading and supported by the experimental results presented in the section.

claim: HCN channels in dendritic field A are implicated in coherence tuning.
source: HCN channels in dendritic field A are implicated in coherence tuning
evidence: The claim is implied by the section heading and supported by the experimental results presented in the section.

claim: HCN channels affect membrane properties and synaptic summation.
source: HCN channels affect membrane properties and synaptic summation
evidence: The claim is implied by the section heading and supported by the experimental results presented in the section.

claim: K+ channels complement HCN channels in generating coherence tuning.
source: K+channels complement HCN channels in generating coherence tuning
evidence: The claim is implied by the section heading and supported by the experimental results presented in the section.

claim: Compartmental modeling highlights the role of K+ and Ca2+ channel inactivation in coherence tuning.
source: Compartmental modeling highlights role of K+ and Ca2+channel inactivation in coherence tuning
evidence: The claim is implied by the section heading and supported by the modeling results presented in the section.

claim: The LGMD can detect the spatial coherence of a simulated impending object, thereby carrying out a computation akin to object segmentation critical for proper escape behavior.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a collision-detecting neuron can detect the spatial coherence of a simulated impending object, thereby carrying out a computation akin to object segmentation critical for proper escape behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing the LGMD's selectivity to spatial coherence and its impact on escape behavior.

claim: At the cellular level, object segmentation relies on a precise selection of the spatiotemporal pattern of synaptic inputs by dendritic membrane potential-activated channels.
source: At the cellular level, object segmentation relies on a precise selection of the spatiotemporal pattern of synaptic inputs by dendritic membrane potential-activated channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing the role of HCN and K+ channels in coherence selectivity.

claim: HCN channels mediate coherence tuning of escape behaviors.
source: HCN channels mediate coherence tuning of escape behaviors
evidence: The claim is implied by the section heading and supported by the experimental results showing the effects of HCN channel blockade on escape behavior.

claim: The selectivity of escape behavior depends on HCN channels enhancing spatially coherent responses.
source: Furthermore, we blocked HCN channels in freely moving animals, demonstrating that the selectivity of escape behavior depends on HCN channels enhancing spatially coherent responses (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The model illustrated in Figure 8 was the simplest that reproduced the wide range of experimental data.
source: The model illustrated in Figure 8 was the simplest that reproduced the wide range of our experimental data.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the modeling results.

claim: Detecting the differences in spatiotemporal patterns of synaptic inputs requires an electrotonically extended arbor.
source: Detecting the differences in spatiotemporal patterns of synaptic inputs requires an electrotonically extended arbor.
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling results showing the importance of dendritic morphology for coherence selectivity.

claim: The specific kinetics and distributions of several channels in the LGMD remain to be characterized.
source: Although the specific kinetics and distributions of several channels in the LGMD remain to be characterized, the model is well grounded (Material and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: After extensive searches through parameter space, no other combinations of mechanisms could be found that reproduced the experimental data as well as the presented model.
source: After extensive searches through parameter space we could not find other combinations of mechanisms that reproduced the experimental data as well.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' modeling efforts.

claim: One likely reason for the model's quantitative discrepancies is that details of the bursting mechanisms may be imperfectly tuned in the model.
source: One likely reason is that details of the bursting mechanisms may be imperfectly tuned in the model, due to the absence of a second calcium-sensitive K+ conductance (Peron and Gabbiani, 2009) or still uncharacterized properties of an M current (unpublished observations).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the authors' assessment of the model's limitations.

claim: HCN channels have long been known to influence dendritic integration in hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: HCN channels have long been known to influence dendritic integration in hippocampal pyramidal neurons (Magee, 1998), and KD as well (Storm, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Magee, 1998 and Storm, 1988.

claim: Dendritic K+ channels have been found to compartmentalize dendrites.
source: More recently, dendritic K+ channels have been found to compartmentalize dendrites, and it has been suggested that spatiotemporal interactions between HCN and K+ channels regulate neuronal excitability (Harnett et al., 2013; Harnett et al., 2015; Mishra and Narayanan, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harnett et al., 2013; Harnett et al., 2015; Mishra and Narayanan, 2015.

claim: It is possible that selectivity for broad spatial synaptic input patterns arises in pyramidal neurons by mechanisms analogous to those described in the LGMD.
source: It is thus possible that selectivity for broad spatial synaptic input patterns arises in pyramidal neurons by mechanisms analogous to those described here.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the similarities between the LGMD and pyramidal neurons.

claim: In thalamocortical neurons, HCN channels influence K+ and Ca2+ channel inactivation, thereby regulating bursting and excitability.
source: In thalamocortical neurons, HCN channels influence K+ and Ca2+ channel inactivation, thereby regulating bursting and excitability (McCormick and Pape, 1990; McCormick, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McCormick and Pape, 1990 and McCormick, 1991.

claim: HCN regulation of bursting has been tied to a rat model of absence epilepsy.
source: HCN regulation of bursting has been tied to a rat model of absence epilepsy (Ludwig et al., 2003; Kole et al., 2007) and may also contribute to human epilepsy (Bender et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ludwig et al., 2003; Kole et al., 2007; and Bender et al., 2003.

claim: HCN-dependent regulation of persistent or burst firing has been involved in working memory.
source: In addition to possible disease states, HCN-dependent regulation of persistent or burst firing has also been involved in working memory (Thuault et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thuault et al., 2013.
